answer: Every facility carries managed-by (system or user, default system); only user-created facilities can be user deleted. trib-ptp, line-ptp, ethernet, otu, odu and flexo-group all report it. The high order ODU is created automatically by the system when an SCH (super-channel) is created, so on a CHM6 with an OTU configured use `show odu` to confirm it exists. The `add odu` page states the pre-condition explicitly: Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added. You then add the low order ODUs by hand, for example `add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu 1-7-L1-1-ODUCni time-slots 1..80`, and the digital service with `add xcon-<name> source <client> destination <line ODU>`; xcon defaults to managed-by user.

`bert` runs the Bit Error Rate Test, in Operational mode: `bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10`, then `bert stop test-id=TestX` (test-id is mandatory on stop), `bert get`, `bert delete`. test-duration minimum is 10 seconds, maximum 1000 hours, and 0 means indefinite. Test patterns are injected on the facility itself: test-signal-type on ethernet and odu-diagnostics takes none (default), PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31 or PRBS31NONINV, with test-signal-direction ingress/egress/both and test-signal-monitoring true/false (default false). Loopbacks are the loopback attribute on otu, odu and ethernet: none (default), facility or terminal, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

At each end the supporting facility must already exist and a secure-entity must be bound to it: `add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <facility> remote-secure-entity <far-end AID> enabled true`. supporting-facility is the optical-carrier on 1830 GX G40, the ODU on G30, or the ODU/OTUflex for CHM7/CHM7X L1 service encryption; remote-secure-entity is the AID of the remote optical carrier, ODU or OTUflex. enabled defaults to false and alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited, so both need attention. IKE re-keying parameters: re-key-frequency 3600..86400 seconds (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy continue-traffic (default) or kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 seconds (default 0). The X.509v3 identities must be imported first with import-certificate: the local-certificate for this node and the far end trusted remote peer certificate as a peer-certificate, plus its trusted-certificate chain.

The `telemetry` command configures the two kinds, persistent and dynamic telemetry; the object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted (`show telemetry`, `set telemetry id <string>`, id up to 4096 characters). `show subscriptions` lists the subscriptions. `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` shows each configured subscription with related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream default, once, poll), updates-only (default false) and user-access. What each one is watching is `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<path-name>`: subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode (target-defined default, on-change, sample), sample-interval and heartbeat-interval in milliseconds (default 0) and suppress-redundant (default true).

`show db-protection-scheme` reports what protects the database at rest: encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which is changed via the db-migrate RPC. Before you can take a copy, the db-passphrase used for snapshot encryption must be configured, either globally with `set security-policies db-passphrase` or inline as `take-snapshot db-passphrase=***`. It requires a minimum of 40 characters (40..200), must contain no dictionary words, and allows special characters from the 85-character Z85 set; automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Then `take-snapshot [db-instance=temp|manual|onehour|oneday|oneweek] [description=]`, list with `show database`, export with `upload database`.

`show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>` tells you whether the prefix reached the route table and where it came from: source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop, which is none for normal routes, or blackhole or unreachable, in which case no next-hop is created under the route. `show rib-<rib-name>` gives the RIB vrf and address-family (ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast); each routing instance gets one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. `show vrf-<name>` identifies the instance, with type mgmt or internal and chassis-name. `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>` gives the resolved next-hop-address, for example `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. On the static route itself, `show ipv4-static-route-<prefix>/<vrf>` reports interface (its VRF must match the route vrf), distance 1..255 (default 1), advertised (default false) and monitoring-state unmonitored/ok/failed.

Password acceptance comes from `security-policies`: strict-password-check (default true) enforces minimum length 8, at least one lower case letter, one upper case letter, one number and one symbol, and the user name cannot be part of the password; when disabled only a 1 character minimum applies. minimum-password-length is 1..200, default 8. enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of the previous 5 passwords, with password-history-size 1..200, default 5. These policies apply only to newly defined passwords. Lockout is per user: max-invalid-login consecutive invalid logins (0..255, default 5) suspends the account for suspension-time (0..1440 minutes, default 5); `show user-<name>` reports user-status lockout and failed-logins, and security-policies has disable-user-lockout. For the stuck session, run `show session`, then `kill-session <ip-address>:<port>`; it cannot be your own session.

`show syslog` defaults: remote-logging-switch true, source-address localhost, log-file-message-coalescence true, log-relay false, assignment-method both, niap-compliant-logging false, privacy-mode false, alarm-report-control allowed. Local files via `log-file` default to source-facilities all with severity informational and above; number-of-files retained defaults to 10 (range 1..20) and max-file-size to 30 MB (range 1..30), and when a file hits max size the oldest files are discarded once the total exceeds number-of-files. The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. Console logging is off by default: log-console enabled false. Remote collectors via `log-server` default to port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, enabled true, source-facilities all. The single switch that turns off everything remote is `set syslog remote-logging-switch false`, which disables all remote logging destinations.

`show alarm` / `show alarms` lists what is raised now, per alarm with resource, AID, alarm-type, direction, location, perceived-severity, reported-time, service-affecting, alarm-category, corrective-action and operator-state; `show current-alarms` gives number-of-alarms and last-changed. Most alarms have automatic raise and clear criteria. The small subset that must be cleared by hand is listed with `show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true` and cleared with `clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [resource=...]`, for example `clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL`; this applies only to system wide alarms not associated with a particular resource. What decides whether inhibiting reporting drops alarms already up is `set alarm-control arc-behavior`: leave-alarms (default) leaves current alarms raised when ARC is set to inhibit, clear-alarms clears them.

The Equipment dashboard shows temperature: `status equipment` lists chassis, cards per chassis with subtype and TOMs per card, with per-equipment temperature sensors and power values plus presence, oper-state and alarms (for example chassis-1 temp 25C, power 2.1/4400 W, card-1-1 temp 25C). To narrow it, give the chassis id as the filter, `status equipment 5`; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so it is either all chassis or exactly one. The underlying sensors come from PM: `show pm` gives real-time temperature (C) for cards, FAN-CTRL and PEM, chassis inlet-temperature, and fan-speed in percent. The physical reflection is the LEDs: `show leds` and `show led status` return led-<location>/<name> with status off, green, yellow, amber, red, their flashing variants, cycling, cycling-with-off or not-available.

`show ots-<name>` describes the line. span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx are the measured span losses based on OSC powers, 0..99 dB where 99 dB means OLOS, versus the configured span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive (0..80 dB, default 0; 99 dB also treated as not configured on receive). span-loss-reference selects which is used, measured (default) or configured. span-loss-alarm-threshold (0..80 dB or 99, default 99) is set autonomously by the system, is persistent across reboot, and can be refreshed with the update command in measured mode. span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0.00..10.00 dB, default 1.0, and feeds the NMC input power range and the span loss high alarm; fiber-length-derived-rx/tx and external-attenuation-rx/tx (0..30 dB) also apply. What the amplifier compensates with is `show amplifier-<name>`: gain-operating and gain-target (0..40 dB), gain-range-actual, control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, gain-adjustment -20..20 dB, span-loss-control (default enabled, and must be enabled when span-loss-reference is measured), tilt-actual, input-power-mon, output-power-mon and control-state.

Going down from the client: trib-ptp is the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver equipment and the immediate protocol layer, and above it sits the client facility (ethernet, fc, stm or a client otu). That is mapped into a low order ODU (`add odu-<name> odu-type ODU4/ODU4i/ODUflexi parent-odu <HO-ODU>`), and the low order ODU is joined to the line by an xcon, whose network-mapping names the server layer (ODUCn, ODUCni, ODU4i, ODUflexi). The high order ODU sits under the line otu / flexo-group, which sits on the line-ptp. The digital to optical handover is at the line-ptp and its optical-carrier: line-system-mode openwave is described as the L1 to L0 local power control that adjusts Tx power from the L1 transponder towards the L0 line-system card (WSS, Mux or Amplifier). Below that, optical-carrier (frequency in MHz, tx-power) grouped into a super-channel is what the L0 domain carries as an nmc on a parent mc or oms, cross connected by an oxcon.

No, they are two different objects. A counter crossing a limit is PM: `add`/`set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]` sets the limit on one instance, and `set pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` sets it per resource type, exposing default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value. Whether the crossing is reported at all is tca-supervision on pm-control-entry, or default-tca-supervision on pm-profile-entry. How loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: `set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value>` with critical, event, major, minor, not-reported or warning, or `set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>` with the same set.

Set the card object: `set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited`; the values are allowed and inhibited. The same alarm-report-control attribute exists on the facilities the card carries (trib-ptp, line-ptp, ethernet, otu, odu, flexo-group, optical-carrier, ots, amplifier), where the default is allowed, so inhibit those too if you want them silent. You can also move the card to `set card-<name> admin-state maintenance`; admin-state takes lock, unlock (default) or maintenance. What happens to the alarms it already raised is decided system wide by `set alarm-control arc-behavior`: leave-alarms, the default, leaves current alarms in a raised mode when ARC is set to inhibit; clear-alarms clears the current alarms.

`show secure-application-<id>` gives type (server or client), status enabled/disabled, active-certificate-id and in-use; in-use is a leafref to active-certificate-id and is the certificate the application presents. Assign it with `set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <cert>`, and multiple are allowed, for example `set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY`. The certificate is a local-certificate, the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing that application identity; import it with `import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=<name> <PEM string> <passphrase>`. Its CA chain must be imported as trusted-certificate first (root certificates must be installed individually; the -i flag imports intermediates from a PEM bundle), otherwise local-certificate status shows untrusted. For TLS mutual authentication set verify-client-cert to required (default disabled). For L1 encryption the far end certificate is imported as a peer-certificate.

Pipe the show command through the display filter: `show pm <command flag> | display csv` outputs CSV data importable into a spreadsheet such as Excel; display xml and display json are also available. Scope it to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter arguments (data-type, parameter, resource, resource-type, AID) and the pm-15min period; bins are selected with -sbin=<number> and -ebin=<number> (default bin 0 is current data and all bins are shown), or by time with -st= and -et= using the format 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00. -t forces a single generic table, -n= caps records per chassis (default 1000) and -s= skips records. To get files off the node instead, `upload pm-logs <file-server> <path> period=pm-15min` uploads PM data logs; without period all periods are included.

`show pm-catalog <string>` shows the contents of the PM catalog for that catalog name, for example `show pm-catalog parameter-undersized`, which returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. The same lookup per parameter is `show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]`, for example `show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds`; `show pm-parameter` on its own lists all PM parameters. Both commands are read only and are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use pm-control: `set pm-control <entity> data-supervision false`. data-supervision is real-time data supervision for that resource and takes true or false, defaulting to true. The documented example is exactly a card: `set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false`. `show pm-control` lists the configuration for all currently existing resources in the system that support PM data. The equivalent per instance attribute is `set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false`, also true/false with default true. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, pm-control-entry is keyed exactly on that scope: `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [data-supervision <value>] [tca-supervision <value>]`, so `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true` turns threshold crossing supervision on for just the 15-minute ingress near-end counters of that one resource. direction takes ingress, egress, all or na (default all); location takes all, na, near-end or far-end (default all); data-supervision and tca-supervision are true or false. `show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> supported-parameters` lists the PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, with a maximum of 100 elements.

`show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]` gives both. type is either counter or gauge. units is one of na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors or MHz. For example `show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized` returns units packets and type counter. `show pm-parameter` with no parameter lists all PM parameters, and `show pm-catalog <name>` returns the same units and type pair from the catalog. The pm-filter description also notes that a PM parameter can be either a counter or a gauge.

Yes: `set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled`. The pm-profile object holds all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. global-data-supervision takes auto-enabled, which globally enables PM data-supervision without having to toggle it individually, or manual, the default, in which the data-supervision flag is controlled via pm-profile-entry or directly per pm-control-entry. Read it back with `show pm-profile`. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

That is pm-profile-entry, which is the PM configuration per resource type: `set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true`. default-data-supervision decides, for newly created resources of that type, whether PM data supervision is automatically enabled; the companion default-tca-supervision does the same for threshold crossing supervision. Both take true or false. direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all, and location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all; period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h. Read them back with the matching `show pm-profile-entry-...`.

`show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset`, for example `show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9`. real-time-data-last-reset is a date-and-time giving the last real time data reset for that resource; if the data was never reset, it is the date and time of that resource creation. The same show also returns resource-type, AID (string, 1..64 characters), real-time-supervision (true/false, default true) and the pm-control-entry children per period, direction and location. The counters themselves are cleared with `clear pm real-time`, optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, AID, period or direction.

Use pm-threshold, which is per instance: `add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/errored-seconds high-threshold <value>`, with set to change it, show to read it and delete to remove it. period is a PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h; direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all; location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all; parameter is the PM parameter identifier, which can be a counter or a gauge. low-threshold and high-threshold accept a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na (not applicable), or not-supported, and both default to na. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

`show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` returns default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold, the system defined default values for that parameter, plus min-value and max-value, the minimum and maximum allowed for the parameter, alongside the currently configured low-threshold and high-threshold. All of these are a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na (not applicable), or not-supported. You write the configured values with set, for example `set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200`. This object is the PM configuration per parameter for a resource type, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.
